orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, still telling Lockwood (in September 1802) what has happened at the Heights since he left. Her story picks up the morning after Easter Monday, in April 1802, the day after Cathy and Hareton made friends.

notes.t: On the morrow of that Monday

notes.g: Keep Cathy, whom I look after, by my side.
Fruit bushes grown for jam and pies.
notes.n: Gooseberries grew in the garden in Chapter II too.

notes.t: an importation of plants from the Grange
notes.g: Bringing plants over from the Grange's gardens.

notes.n: A phrase from the Bible (Psalm 17: 'Keep me as the apple of the eye').

notes.t: a fine explosion on the head of it
notes.g: A big row because of it.
The place of the lady of the house at table.
Cutting up the meat to serve.
Oatmeal boiled in water or milk, a breakfast staple.
What devil has got into you.

notes.n: Notice how Cathy's eyes in particular upset him. Nelly explains why later in this chapter.

notes.g: Rechewing half-digested food, as cows do.

notes.e: wi’ a hammer in th’ road!
notes.tr: I must have my wages, and I must go! I had meant to die where I'd served for sixty years. I thought I'd carry my books up to the attic, and all my bits of things, and they could have the kitchen to themselves, for the sake of peace. It was hard to give up my own fireside, but I thought I could do that! But now she's taken my garden from me, and by my heart, master, I can't stand it! You may bow down under the yoke if you like; I'm not used to it, and an old man doesn't soon get used to new burdens. I'd rather earn my food and drink breaking stones on the road!

notes.n: Joseph has worked at the Heights since long before Heathcliff came.

notes.g: Hearthstone: his own place by the fire.
By my heart: a mild oath.

notes.t: bend to th’ yoak an ye will
notes.g: Submit like an ox under the yoke, if you want to.
notes.n: A yoke is the wooden frame that harnesses oxen. Joseph means Heathcliff may put up with Cathy's rule, but he won't.

notes.t: arn my bite an’ my sup
wi’ a hammer in th’ road
notes.g: Breaking stones to mend the roads.
notes.n: The hardest, lowest-paid work, often given to paupers.

notes.g: A small cellar or cupboard where coal is stored.

notes.tr: It's not Nelly! I wouldn't leave on account of Nelly, nasty good-for-nothing as she is. Thank God, she can't steal anybody's soul! She was never so good-looking that a man couldn't look at her without blinking. It's that frightful, shameless hussy who has bewitched our lad with her bold eyes and her forward ways, till... No! It fairly bursts my heart! He's forgotten everything I've done for him and made of him, and gone and torn up a whole row of the finest currant bushes in the garden!

notes.n: 'Nowt' (nothing) here means a worthless person.

notes.t: a body mud look at her ’bout winking
notes.g: A person might look at her without blinking.
notes.n: A backhanded joke: Nelly was never beautiful enough to dazzle anyone.
'Een' is an old plural of 'eye'.

notes.g: Made of him; how I brought him up.
Overcome by emotion; unable to stay composed.
The danger to Hareton's soul, as Joseph sees it.
notes.n: He believes Cathy has bewitched the lad.

notes.t: to touch a stick about the place
notes.g: To touch anything at all here.

notes.t: you have taken all my land
notes.g: Heathcliff has kept the Linton estate that should have been hers.
notes.n: See the end of Chapter XXX.

notes.g: Rude, worthless girl: a brutal insult.
notes.m: 'Slut' then mainly meant a dirty, slovenly woman, but it was still very offensive.

notes.t: And Hareton’s land, and his money
notes.g: Hareton should have inherited the Heights from his father Hindley.
notes.n: Hindley mortgaged every yard of land to Heathcliff to pay his gambling debts, so Heathcliff took the property when Hindley died (Chapter XVII).

notes.g: Stir him up to turn against me.

notes.m: 'Passion' here means a fit of anger, not love or enthusiasm.

notes.t: seeking his bread where he can get it
notes.n: A threat to throw Hareton out with nothing.

notes.m: At the Heights 'the house' is the big family room, not the whole building.

notes.t: her father-in-law’s conduct to his father
notes.g: How Heathcliff treated Hindley, Hareton's father.
notes.n: Hindley gambled away all his land to Heathcliff (see Chapter XVII).

notes.g: Against him; to run him down.

notes.t: took the master’s reputation home to himself
notes.g: Felt any attack on Heathcliff as an attack on himself.
notes.n: Heathcliff has raised Hareton since he was a small child.

notes.g: The man who treats her cruelly (Heathcliff).

notes.m: 'Several' here means each their own, not 'a few'.

notes.g: Cathy's runaway ride to Penistone Crags, when Nelly found her at the Heights.
notes.n: See Chapter XVIII. Hareton was then a rough, unlettered lad.

notes.t: he was twenty-three and she eighteen
notes.g: Hareton was born in 1778 and Cathy in 1784, so this is spring 1802.
They both have the first Catherine's eyes.
notes.n: Hareton is her nephew (her brother Hindley's son) and Cathy is her daughter. This explains Heathcliff's reaction to Cathy's eyes earlier, and his words about Hareton's face in Chapter XXXI.

notes.g: Young Cathy, as opposed to her mother.
Destroy both families, the Earnshaws and the Lintons.
notes.n: 'House' means both building and family line.

notes.g: Labouring like the Greek hero famous for his superhuman strength.
notes.n: Hercules performed twelve impossible tasks, the 'Labours of Hercules'.

notes.t: lift a slate off either roof
notes.n: Roofs here were covered in heavy stone slates.

notes.g: Their heirs: Hareton for Hindley, Cathy for Edgar.
Some great change he senses coming.
notes.n: Keep in mind that Nelly has already told Lockwood Heathcliff had a 'queer' end (Chapter XXXII).

notes.g: His own young self in human form.
notes.n: Like Heathcliff once, Hareton has been kept ignorant and made a farm labourer by the man who took his inheritance.

notes.g: Spoken to him in a sensible way.
Powerful enough to grip my mind.

notes.n: The plural of 'memorandum', a note to help you remember.
After old Mr. Earnshaw died, Hindley made Heathcliff a farm labourer and denied him schooling (Chapter VI).

notes.g: An obsession with one single subject.
notes.n: A fashionable medical term in the 1840s, when the novel was written.

notes.g: A feeling that something is about to happen.

notes.n: In Chapter XXIX Heathcliff said Joseph believed his conscience was 'playing the fiend inside' him.
